§9.6.3 Cell Text Fidelity

📄 Page rule — applied from the page alone

tables-cell-text-fidelity · tables fidelity ocr

✅ Normative

The text of a cell MUST be what the rendered page shows — not the text layer, not OCR, and not what the value ought to be. A character that cannot be read at any zoom MUST be written as [illegible], never as a plausible guess.

The text layer and the rendered image disagree at the character level far more often than expected, and the cost of a single wrong digit depends entirely on who reads the table. The text layer is a hint about roughly what is there; the image decides.

Three cells that were read wrong

In each of these the transcription and the OCR agreed with each other — and a zoomed view of the page proved both wrong:

printed 0.99        → transcribed 0.98      (Age-to-Ultimate factor)
printed 2012.5-(A)  → transcribed 2013.5-(A)
printed 1.0400^(W)  → transcribed 1.04009^(W)

A disputed cell SHOULD be settled from a zoomed crop of the cell or from the word coordinates, and MUST NOT be settled by plausibility. "Plausible" is exactly what produced all three errors above: 0.98 is a perfectly reasonable factor.

What is printed is what is written

  • Typos stay. A word misspelled inside a cell MUST keep its misspelling.
  • Numbers are copied digit by digit, with thousands and decimal separators exactly as printed. See Accounting Number Formats§9.6.1.
  • Wrapped codes are not fused with their neighbours. In a narrow column a code can wrap onto two lines, or two short codes can sit in neighbouring cells and look like one. The column boundaries and the cell's span decide: fusing B-2 with VC, or TR-1 with TR-2, is an error, and it also throws off the column count of the whole row.
  • A blank cell stays empty. A cell that prints nothing MUST be rendered empty; a dash MUST NOT be supplied because the column has dashes elsewhere.

Characters the image cannot tell apart

Some characters are visually identical and no zoom separates them: µ (U+00B5) and μ (U+03BC), a non-breaking space and an ordinary space, a minus sign and a hyphen.

  • The output MUST keep the visible form and the character count exactly as printed, and SHOULD use the character normally typed for that glyph.
  • The text layer MUST NOT be used to break the tie: it is a hint about the content, never the authority on it.
  • A consumer or checker MUST treat the members of each family below as equal, so the choice among them cannot make an output non-conforming.
Family Written as
µ (U+00B5) ≡ μ (U+03BC) either
non-breaking space ≡ ordinary space an ordinary space
minus sign (U+2212) ≡ hyphen-minus -
non-breaking hyphen ≡ hyphen-minus -
figure dash, en dash ≡ hyphen, inside a numeric range either

The image outranks every other source on what is printed. Where two codepoints are indistinguishable there is no fact about the page for it to be authoritative over — µ and μ are the same ink. The visible form is fidelity and stays exact; the codepoint underneath is a serialisation detail.

A dash that is doing something is not a homoglyph question. An em dash alone in a cell is a value — see Marks and Symbols in Cells§9.6.6 — and a struck-through digit is not a character variant at all.

✅ Sample — a true minus sign

−742 and −2,710 are set with a true minus sign rather than a hyphen, beside — for nil. The minus sign is written as the hyphen-minus -; the em dashes stay em dashes. The header cells are genuinely merged across two rows and wrapped labels are joined; the Net Sales and Other Items bands are bold where the headings are not.

What else rests on the image

  • Duplicated Tables§9.2.4 — the rendered page decides whether a repeated table is really printed twice.
  • Struck and Replaced Values§9.6.7 — OCR silently joins a struck value to its replacement and produces a number that appears nowhere on the page. Only the image catches it.
